source.title: ObserverBench: Testing Mechanistic Estimates for Intervention and Control

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses SAE-feature probes as safety-monitoring methods and reports their APPS performance, but it does not test SAE reconstruction error or the dark-matter claims.
record.gate_note: The SAE monitoring results are not results about reconstruction error, its linear predictability or scaling, replacing activations with reconstructions, or retaining an error term in mechanistic analyses. The APPS SAE-probe outcomes are recorded as adjacent findings with versions ["none"]. Other APPS monitoring results and the paper’s control and intervention-prediction experiments do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper uses SAE features and reconstructions only as inputs to APPS safety monitors and reports their AUROC and audit violations against dense residual probes. It never measures SAE reconstruction error, its linear predictability or scaling across sizes, the loss effect of splicing in reconstructions, or how much model behaviour is lost without an error term. It neither cites nor tests the dark-matter paper. T4 is kept because SAEs serve as a tool whose monitoring performance is scored, but none of V1–V6 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that observer adequacy is task-relative and that AUROC and realized violations can rank monitors differently. They add that the best activation context changes between checkpoints and that a sparser SAE readout need not improve the decision. They explicitly limit the SAE results to the tested checkpoint, layer, task and probing rule, with disclosed mismatches.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce or test the original dark-matter analysis. Its SAE-related work applies sparse probing and official SAE probes to APPS safety monitoring.
record.method_sensitivity: The APPS results vary by model/checkpoint and monitor context. The Qwen3.5 SAE comparison uses a base-trained SAE on a post-trained model; the Qwen2.5 SAE diagnostic reports observed mean L0 = 115 versus reported 240.

fits_no_version.finding: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct layer 19, a logistic monitor on BatchTopK SAE reconstructions scores AUROC 0.954 with 4.79 mean violations. The dense residual monitor on the same layer scores 0.983 with 2.05.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Probes on SAE reconstructions lose task-relevant linearly readable information compared with the full residual. This holds under an off-distribution SAE (observed L0 115 vs reported 240).

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-feature probes trail dense residual probes on APPS backdoor monitoring. On Qwen2.5 the sparse readout has 4.67 vs 2.05 violations. On Gemma, Gemma Scope scores 0.870 vs 0.969 AUROC and 9.07 vs 2.18 violations. On Qwen3.5, a base-trained Qwen-Scope SAE scores 0.811 vs 0.936 AUROC and 12.7 vs 6.6 violations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE-feature readouts underperform dense residual readouts for safety monitoring in these settings. This is a probing-utility result, not a dark-matter test.

record.problems: The SAE comparisons are limited to particular APPS tasks and probing rules. The authors disclose a Qwen2.5 activation-density mismatch (observed mean L0 = 115 versus reported 240) and a Qwen3.5 base-to-posttraining SAE checkpoint mismatch; they explicitly caution against generalizing these findings to SAE features broadly.
record.rows_left_out: No other SAE-monitor results were left out. The remaining study results do not apply or measure SAE error or dark matter.

untested.parts: No regression of SAE error on input activations.
No per-token error norms, no SAE size sweep, no shared failure contexts.
No splicing of reconstructions into the forward pass and no comparison of loss against random errors of the same size.
No split of the error into linear and nonlinear parts.
No circuit or steering analysis with versus without an SAE error term. The probe on reconstructions is adjacent only.
No comparison of SAE architectures or training objectives on error. The L0 mismatch and the base-to-post-trained checkpoint mismatch are disclosed but not studied.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are given because the study tests no version. The reconstruction-probe rows (R4/R5) come closest to V5's idea that the error carries information. They concern linear probe readability, not model computation, so they stay under fits_no_version. The record's T4/uses_without_test is retained, but T6 is defensible since the dark-matter finding itself is never used or cited.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not measure whether SAE error vectors are linear functions of input activations.
The paper does not measure per-token SAE error norms across SAE sizes, shared failure contexts, or whether error persists with scale.
The paper does not replace model activations with SAE reconstructions or compare the resulting model loss with matched random errors.
The paper does not separate linear and nonlinear SAE error or test their relationship to learned features or further dictionary learning.

The paper compares SAE-based safety-monitor readouts with dense residual monitors, but does not test whether keeping an SAE error term preserves model behavior in circuit, steering, or related analyses.
The paper notes SAE/checkpoint and activation-density mismatches, but does not test whether training choices cause dark matter or whether better architectures or end-to-end training reduce it.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.note: The reconstruction is used as a monitor input; the study does not measure reconstruction error or replace the model's activations with the reconstruction.
rows.check: The probe is fit on SAE reconstructions, so the gap to the dense probe (4.79 vs 2.05 violations) reflects readable information lost in the error term. It measures probe readout, not model behaviour under circuit or steering analysis, so it does not bear on V5. Kept as an adjacent finding.
